questions.question: What does Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) primarily automate?

options.text: RDS database backups
Creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots and AMIs
S3 object versioning
CloudWatch log retention

explanation.correct: DLM automates the lifecycle of EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs — creation, retention, copy, and deletion.
explanation.why: A is AWS Backup for RDS; C is S3 Lifecycle rules; D is CloudWatch Logs retention settings.

questions.question: Where do you find Amazon DLM in the AWS Management Console?

options.text: S3 → Management → Lifecycle
EC2 → Elastic Block Store → Lifecycle Manager
AWS Backup → Backup Plans
CloudWatch → Events → Rules

explanation.correct: DLM is located under EC2 → Elastic Block Store → Lifecycle Manager in the console.
explanation.why: A is for S3 object lifecycle; C is AWS Backup service; D is CloudWatch Events.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about DLM pricing?

options.text: DLM charges per lifecycle policy created
DLM charges per snapshot taken
DLM is a free service — you only pay for snapshot storage
DLM charges per GB of snapshot data transferred

explanation.correct: The DLM service itself is free. You only pay for the EBS snapshot storage in Amazon S3.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are incorrect — DLM has no per-policy, per-snapshot, or per-GB service charges.

questions.question: What is the minimum snapshot frequency supported by Amazon DLM?

options.text: 5 minutes
15 minutes
30 minutes
1 hour

explanation.correct: The minimum frequency for DLM snapshots is 1 hour. You cannot schedule more frequent snapshots using DLM.
explanation.why: Options A, B, and C are below the minimum supported interval.

questions.question: How does DLM identify which EBS volumes to target for snapshots?

options.text: By volume size
By Availability Zone
By resource tags
By EC2 instance type

explanation.correct: DLM uses tag-based selection. You specify a tag key-value pair and DLM snapshots all volumes matching that tag.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are not the selection criteria — DLM relies entirely on resource tags.

questions.question: What are the two main policy types in Amazon DLM?

options.text: Volume policy and Instance policy
EBS snapshot policy and EBS-backed AMI policy
Custom policy and Managed policy
Scheduled policy and Event-based policy

explanation.correct: DLM supports EBS snapshot policies (for volumes) and EBS-backed AMI policies (for creating AMIs from instances).
explanation.why: A and D describe resource types or trigger types, not the official policy type names in DLM.

questions.question: What does count-based retention mean in a DLM policy?

options.text: Delete snapshots older than N days
Keep only the most recent N snapshots and delete older ones
Create N snapshots per day
Limit total snapshot size to N GB

explanation.correct: Count-based retention keeps the last N snapshots. When a new snapshot is created that exceeds the count, the oldest is automatically deleted.
explanation.why: A describes age-based retention; C describes schedule frequency; D is not a DLM feature.

questions.question: A team needs backups in two separate AWS regions for compliance. Which DLM feature handles this?

options.text: Multi-AZ snapshot
Cross-region copy
Snapshot replication
S3 cross-region replication

explanation.correct: DLM's cross-region copy feature automatically copies snapshots to a target region after creation.
explanation.why: A is not a DLM feature; C is not a DLM term; D applies to S3 objects, not EBS snapshots.

questions.question: What is an EBS snapshot?

options.text: A full copy of an EBS volume stored locally on EC2
A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume stored in Amazon S3
A live mirror of an EBS volume in another AZ
A compressed archive of EC2 instance files

explanation.correct: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup stored in Amazon S3. AWS manages the S3 storage — it is not visible in your S3 buckets.
explanation.why: A is wrong (stored in S3, not locally); C describes multi-attach or replication; D is not accurate.

questions.question: Why are EBS snapshots cost-efficient to store over time?

options.text: AWS compresses snapshots using ZIP format
Snapshots are stored in Glacier automatically
Snapshots are incremental — only changed blocks are stored after the first
AWS deletes duplicate blocks across accounts

explanation.correct: EBS snapshots are incremental. After the first full snapshot, subsequent ones only store blocks that changed, significantly reducing storage cost.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are incorrect — incremental storage is the actual reason.

questions.question: Which IAM role does DLM use by default when creating policies?

options.text: AmazonEC2FullAccess
AWSDataLifecycleManagerDefaultRole
AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole
EC2SnapshotRole

explanation.correct: DLM creates and uses AWSDataLifecycleManagerDefaultRole by default. This role grants DLM permission to create and delete snapshots.
explanation.why: A is too broad; C is for AWS Backup service; D is not a real default role name.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Custom policy and a Default policy in DLM?

options.text: Default policy is free; custom policy is paid
Custom policy is only for AMIs; default is for snapshots
Default policy uses pre-configured settings; custom policy lets you define all parameters
There is no difference — they produce the same result

explanation.correct: Default policies use pre-configured sensible settings and automatically back up volumes/instances without recent backups. Custom policies give you full control over all parameters.
explanation.why: A is wrong (both are free); B is wrong (both support snapshots and AMIs); D is wrong (they differ in configurability).

questions.question: A company runs a critical database on EC2 with an EBS volume. Their RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is 4 hours. What DLM schedule should they configure?

options.text: Every 24 hours
Every 4 hours
Every 1 hour
Every 12 hours

explanation.correct: An RPO of 4 hours means the maximum acceptable data loss is 4 hours. Snapshots must be taken every 4 hours to meet this requirement.
explanation.why: 24 hours or 12 hours would exceed the RPO; 1 hour is more frequent than needed (though not wrong, it's over-engineering for this RPO).

questions.question: You create a DLM policy targeting tag Env=Production with count-based retention of 7. After running for 10 days, how many snapshots exist?

explanation.correct: Count-based retention of 7 keeps the last 7 snapshots at any time. On day 8, snapshot 1 is deleted. On day 10, only days 4-10 exist (7 snapshots).
explanation.why: A is wrong — retention cleanup runs automatically. C and D don't match the retention count.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios is NOT a good fit for Amazon DLM?

options.text: Automating nightly backups of 100 EBS volumes
Ensuring snapshots are available in us-east-1 after being created in ap-south-1
Automating RDS database snapshots on a schedule
Deleting snapshots older than 90 days automatically

explanation.correct: DLM manages EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs only. RDS automated snapshots are managed by RDS itself, not DLM.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all valid DLM use cases. C is the exception — RDS has its own snapshot automation.

questions.question: You want to tag every DLM-created snapshot with CostCenter=BackupTeam for billing visibility. Which DLM feature enables this?

options.text: Tag propagation from the source volume
Resource tagging in the DLM policy schedule configuration
AWS Cost Explorer tag filter
S3 object tagging

explanation.correct: DLM allows you to define tags that are automatically applied to every snapshot it creates. This is configured in the schedule settings of the policy.
explanation.why: A refers to volume tags (which can also be copied but require enabling); C is a reporting tool; D applies to S3 objects.

questions.question: What is the difference between age-based and count-based retention in DLM?

options.text: Age-based is for AMIs; count-based is for snapshots
Age-based deletes snapshots older than N days; count-based keeps only the last N snapshots
Age-based keeps N snapshots; count-based deletes after N days
They are equivalent — just different names for the same behavior

explanation.correct: Age-based retention deletes snapshots older than N days, weeks, or months. Count-based retention keeps only the most recent N snapshots.
explanation.why: A is wrong (both can be used for either type); C reverses the definitions; D is wrong (they behave differently).

questions.question: A DLM policy has been created but no snapshots appear after 48 hours. Which is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: DLM does not work in all AWS regions
The target EBS volumes are missing the tag specified in the policy
DLM requires manual triggering for the first snapshot
Cross-region copy must be enabled before snapshots can be created

explanation.correct: The most common reason for no snapshots is that the target volumes do not have the tag key-value pair specified in the DLM policy. DLM silently finds zero matching resources.
explanation.why: A is false; C is false (DLM is fully automatic); D is false (cross-region copy is optional and independent of initial snapshot creation).

questions.question: Which AWS service should you use if you need to back up both EBS volumes AND RDS databases under a single backup policy?

options.text: Amazon DLM
Amazon S3 Lifecycle
AWS Backup
AWS CloudFormation

explanation.correct: AWS Backup is a centralized service that manages backups across multiple AWS services including EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, and more. DLM only covers EBS snapshots and AMIs.
explanation.why: A only handles EBS/AMIs; B is for S3 objects; D is infrastructure as code.

questions.question: Your organization uses DLM to snapshot 200 volumes daily. Each snapshot takes 4 hours to complete. Does this cause any issues?

options.text: Yes — DLM can only process 10 snapshots concurrently
Yes — snapshots taking longer than 1 hour are cancelled
No — DLM initiates all snapshots at the scheduled time; they complete asynchronously
No — DLM queues snapshots and processes them one at a time

explanation.correct: DLM initiates snapshot creation at the scheduled time for all matching volumes. The EC2 API handles snapshot creation asynchronously — there is no DLM-level concurrency limit for initiating snapshots.
explanation.why: A and B are incorrect; D is partially wrong — they are initiated concurrently, not serially.

questions.question: A DLM policy uses count-based retention of 5 and creates 1 snapshot per day. After 30 days, the policy is disabled. What happens to existing snapshots?

options.text: All snapshots are deleted immediately
The 5 most recent snapshots are deleted; older ones are kept
Existing snapshots are retained indefinitely — DLM only stops creating new ones
Snapshots are converted to AMIs automatically

explanation.correct: Disabling a DLM policy stops future snapshot creation. It does NOT delete existing snapshots. Those remain until manually deleted or until the policy is re-enabled and retention enforcement runs.
explanation.why: A is wrong — disabling never deletes existing snapshots. B and D are not accurate behaviors.

questions.question: You need DLM snapshots in us-east-1 to be available in eu-west-1 within 15 minutes of creation for a near-zero RTO. Is DLM cross-region copy the right tool?

options.text: Yes — DLM cross-region copy completes within 2 minutes
Yes — DLM is designed for sub-minute cross-region copy
No — cross-region snapshot copy time depends on snapshot size and network; DLM does not guarantee a specific copy SLA
No — DLM cross-region copy is only available for AMIs, not snapshots

explanation.correct: DLM cross-region copy initiates the copy but the time to complete depends on snapshot size and AWS network conditions. It is not a guaranteed SLA and may not meet strict 15-minute RTO requirements for large volumes.
explanation.why: A and B are incorrect — AWS does not guarantee specific copy completion times. D is wrong — cross-region copy works for both snapshots and AMIs.

questions.question: A lifecycle policy is configured with 2 schedules: Schedule A runs daily with 7-count retention; Schedule B runs weekly with 4-count retention. After 4 weeks, how many snapshots from Schedule B exist?

explanation.correct: Schedule B runs weekly with count-based retention of 4. After 4 weeks, 4 snapshots exist (weeks 1-4). When week 5 runs, week 1 is deleted, maintaining the count of 4.
explanation.why: 28 and 7 ignore retention; 2 doesn't match the configured retention count.

questions.question: Which statement is true about DLM policies and IAM permissions?

options.text: DLM uses the AWS account root user credentials to create snapshots
DLM uses a service-linked role that is created automatically when you first create a policy
You must manually create and attach an IAM role to every DLM policy
DLM does not require any IAM permissions to function

explanation.correct: DLM uses a service-linked role (or the default IAM role AWSDataLifecycleManagerDefaultRole). When you create your first policy, AWS automatically creates this role if it doesn't exist.
explanation.why: A is a major security violation — DLM never uses root. C is partially true for custom roles but the default setup is automatic. D is false — IAM permissions are required.

questions.question: A compliance requirement states that all production backups must be immutable for 90 days — even system administrators cannot delete them. Can DLM enforce this?

options.text: Yes — enable the immutable snapshot setting in the DLM policy schedule
Yes — set the retention type to locked and specify 90 days
Partially — DLM can create the snapshots, but snapshot immutability requires enabling snapshot lock on EBS snapshots separately
No — DLM has no immutability features at all

explanation.correct: EBS snapshot lock (a separate feature) enables immutability on snapshots, preventing deletion even by administrators. DLM creates the snapshots on schedule, and snapshot lock can be applied to protect them. These two features are used together.
explanation.why: A and B describe features that do not exist in DLM itself. D is partially wrong — DLM plays a role but snapshot lock is the enforcement mechanism.

questions.question: What happens when two DLM policies target the same EBS volume?

options.text: An error is thrown — one policy must be deleted
The newer policy overrides the older one
Both policies run independently — the volume gets snapshots from both schedules
AWS automatically merges the two policies into one

explanation.correct: DLM policies are independent. If two policies both target the same volume tag, both run on their respective schedules and create separate snapshots. This can be intentional (e.g., different retention strategies) or accidental.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all incorrect — there is no conflict resolution or merging.

questions.question: A security audit requires that all EBS snapshots be encrypted at rest. How do you enforce this with DLM?

options.text: Enable encryption in the DLM policy settings
Use AWS KMS to encrypt the source EBS volumes; snapshots inherit the encryption status
Apply an S3 bucket policy requiring encryption on the snapshot storage bucket
DLM does not support encrypted snapshots

explanation.correct: EBS snapshots inherit the encryption status of their source volume. If the EBS volume is encrypted (using AWS KMS), all snapshots DLM creates will also be encrypted automatically.
explanation.why: A is not an option in DLM; C is wrong (snapshot S3 storage is not user-accessible); D is false.

questions.question: You have DLM creating daily snapshots. You manually delete a snapshot that was created 2 days ago. What does DLM do at the next scheduled run?

options.text: DLM detects the missing snapshot and re-creates it
DLM fails and enters an error state
DLM continues creating the next scheduled snapshot normally; the manually deleted snapshot is gone permanently
DLM pauses until you confirm the deletion was intentional

explanation.correct: DLM does not track manual deletions. It simply creates the next snapshot at the scheduled time. The manually deleted snapshot is gone and DLM does not attempt to recreate it.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all incorrect — DLM has no awareness of manual snapshot deletions.

questions.question: What is the correct order of events when a DLM policy runs?

options.text: Retention check → Create snapshot → Apply tags → Cross-region copy
Create snapshot → Apply tags → Retention check → Cross-region copy
Cross-region copy → Create snapshot → Apply tags → Retention check
Apply tags → Create snapshot → Retention check → Cross-region copy

explanation.correct: DLM first creates the new snapshot, applies configured tags to it, then enforces retention by deleting old snapshots, and finally initiates cross-region copy if configured.
explanation.why: A, C, and D have incorrect orderings — retention check and cross-region copy both happen after snapshot creation.

questions.question: A team uses cron expressions in DLM to schedule snapshots at variable times. Which of the following is a valid use case for this over fixed frequency scheduling?

options.text: When snapshots must run exactly at month-end — the last day of each month
When snapshots must run every 30 minutes
When snapshots must be created in a different region
When you want to exclude weekends from the snapshot schedule

explanation.correct: Cron expressions allow complex scheduling like 'last day of the month' which fixed frequency cannot achieve. Month-end snapshots for billing reconciliation are a classic use case.
explanation.why: B is below DLM minimum frequency; C is handled by cross-region copy feature not scheduling; D is also achievable with cron but A is the most precise and specific valid answer.
